The part of the job nobody believes is difficult is the summary. Three people have spoken for forty minutes and I have ninety seconds to say what each of them thinks, while all three are sitting there.
And any verb you choose is a judgement. If you say one of them conceded, you have told the audience she was under pressure.
Exactly that. Conceded, acknowledged and agreed report the same three seconds of audio and hand the listener three different scenes.
So what do you use when you genuinely do not want to take a side?
Said. And said is not neutral either, it is just the least loaded thing available. What I try hardest to avoid is a caricature, because a caricature always gets a laugh and it always misrepresents.
Do you ever check the summary with them afterwards?
During, if I can. I say let me paraphrase you and stop me if I get it wrong. Nobody ever objects to being asked, and about one time in five they stop me.
Which is a considerably higher error rate than any of us would admit to in ordinary conversation.
Let me paraphrase you, and stop me if I get it wrong.
She contends that the design is wrong, and she conceded that the results are real.
That is the gist of it, and it does not do justice to the second half.
I am not putting words in your mouth — tell me if I have.
The first half holds water. The second half does not.

Let me try to sum up, and please stop me if I get any of this wrong. Our first speaker contends that the scheme has worked, and that the cost being quoted by its critics is exaggerated by roughly a third. Our second speaker conceded at the start that waiting times have fallen, which I do not think anybody expected her to concede, and her objection is to the design rather than to the result. And our third speaker claims that the underlying data are unreliable. I have used the word claims deliberately, and I want to say why. He has not produced the alternative figures, and until he does, claims is the honest verb. If he produces them next week, I will use a different one.

The verb we argue about most in this building is claimed. Some people will tell you it is neutral. It is not. Claimed tells the reader, quietly, that you should not believe this person, and once you notice it you cannot stop noticing it. My test is simple and slightly uncomfortable. Would I use the same verb about somebody I agreed with? If the answer is no, I change it. And there is one that slips past everybody, including me, and it is point out. She pointed out that the date was wrong. That does not report a claim, it asserts a fact and attributes it, in three words, and nobody in the room ever objects to it because it sounds like a small polite verb. It is not a small polite verb. It is a verdict.

Nora says the difficult part of her job is summarising three speakers in ninety seconds. He observes that any verb she chooses is already a judgement. She agrees, and explains that conceded, acknowledged and agreed produce three different scenes. He asks what she uses when she does not want to take a side. She answers that she uses said, and that even said is not neutral.
